To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the addition of a polyogenic risk score for coronary artery disease to pooled cohort equations, was associated with a modest improvement in the predictive ability for incident coronary artery disease, and improved risk stratifications for only a small percentage of individuals.

the addition of the polyogenic risk score for CAD (PRS-CAD) to the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) was associated with a modest improvement in the discrimination of incident CAD (C statistic: 0.61 for PRS-CAD vs 0.76 for PCE vs 0.78 for PRS-CADD + PCE).

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the polygenic risk prediction model for CAD is not yet ready for clinical use.

the addition of a polygenetic score to the existing clinical risk score (pooled cohort equations) does not improve risk prediction of coronary artery disease (as measured by the area under the receiver operating curve) but does improve risk stratification of a small proportion of the general population.
polygenic risk scores have limited value for risk prediction in CAD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the polygenic risk scores for CAD did not improve prediction of CAD beyond the PCE model, but did improve the risk stratification of a small number of individuals.
the polygenic risk scores are not ready for clinical application, but they are a promising tool to be used in future research.

polygenic risk scores are useful to identify individuals who are at the highest or lowest risk of developing coronary heart disease, however, they are not useful for individuals in the middle of the risk range.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of a polygeneric risk score for CAD in addition to the pooled cohort equations did not improve the discrimination or calibration of the model.

polygenic risk scores have limited incremental value for CAD risk prediction in addition to the pooled cohort equations, but they do improve risk stratification for a small proportion of the general population.
the addition of a polygenetic score to a clinical risk score is not a panacea.
